title: Kent Beck and the Origins of TDD and Extreme Programming
explainer: Kent Beck developed the write-a-failing-test-first discipline practiced in this lesson while working on Chrysler's C3 payroll project in the late 1990s, and later formalized it in his 2002 book 'Test-Driven Development: By Example.' Beck has said he didn't invent the idea from scratch so much as rediscover a test-first style described in an older programming book; what he and collaborators like Ward Cunningham did was build an entire methodology, Extreme Programming, around short feedback loops, of which TDD was one practice. Beck was also one of the seventeen signatories of the 2001 Agile Manifesto, part of why 'test-first' spread well beyond his own projects.

title: JUnit's Origin Story: A Flight, Not a Committee (1997)
explainer: The xUnit-style framework pattern underneath tools like JUnit and most modern test runners has a specific origin: Kent Beck and Erich Gamma (one of the Gang of Four) built the first version of JUnit together on a flight to the 1997 OOPSLA conference, pair-programming it test-first before carrying the idea over to Java. Beck had already written an earlier Smalltalk testing framework called SUnit, and JUnit's assert-based structure is a direct descendant of it. That a tool this foundational to daily testing practice started as an in-flight side project is a useful reminder of how informally some lasting engineering infrastructure gets built.
